messages.subject: transformed variables in lm
messages.body_plain:
To consider a model with transformed variables,
does it make a difference if I created transformed
variables in my data first, or transform within the
lm function? For instance, say log(y)~x+x^2+ log(x)+...
I can either do:
lm(log(y)~x+I(x^2)+....)

or, transform the variables
mydata$logy<-log(mydata$y)
mydata$xsq<-mydata$x^2
etc
then run lm(logy~x+xsq+ ...)

Does it matter which version I do? I tested this
on a small example and the summary outputs were the
same.

Are there cases where S+ knowing that a variable is squared
(via I(x^2)) or logged, makes a difference in its internal
computations?

Thanks.

--Laura Chihara

messages.subject: Re: transformed variables in lm
messages.body_plain:
Laura,
  It makes no difference at all to the computations--the model matrix 
would be the same in either case. It only matters to the user (see note 1 
below).
  Many users like to 'see' their data or have used packages that require 
the user to create columns in the data set. They will prefer creating 
columns in the data set.
  Other users will enjoy the flexibility of being able to specify 
transforms 'on the fly' and not having to add potentially useless columns 
to the data set. using this approach has an additional advantage--the 
transforms are self documenting. For example, there is no question about 
whether the common or natural log transform was used when you get back to 
looking at your data one year after doing the analysis. A further 
advantage is that the user will not need to create additional columns in a 
prediction data set, if that is intended.
  Note 1: timeDate data must be converted to a numeric format before using 
those data in a regression model.
  Note 2: the poly() function can be useful for building polynomial models 
with a single explanatory variable. It's usefulness decreases when 
additional explanatory variables are added because the poly.transform() 
function can't back-transform the coefficients to reflect the original 
units. Back transformation is only important if it is necessary to report 
the regression model in the original units.
  Hope this helps.
Dave

messages.subject: Future of S-Plus???
messages.body_plain:
Hi, folks:

I suppose that this is a philosophical question.  But at our institution
there are fewer and fewer individuals renewing their S-Plus licenses,
and the consequence is that our individual costs for a renewal license
are escalating.  Of course, this is because R is available free.  I can
just as easily do any analysis in R that I want to do in S-Plus.  But I
still like the ease of graphics in S-Plus, so I continue to use it.  

But it seems to me, also, that TIBCO is not particularly interested in
keeping S-Plus going.  They are, understandably, more interested in
pushing their Spotfire front end, which as you all know now will run R
programs as well as S-Plus programs.

So my question is:  What is the future of S-Plus?  Should I just abandon
it in favor of R?  

TIBCO, what are your plans with respect to S-Plus as more and more folks
migrate to R?

L. G. Hunsicker, M.D.
Professor, Internal Medicine
U. Iowa College of Medicine
Phone:  (319) 356-4763
Fax:  (319) 356-7488
lawrence-hunsicker at uiowa.edu

messages.subject: Re: Future of S-Plus???
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I also would hate to see Splus disappear.  I also prefer the look and feel
of Splus over R.  But my main reason in favor of Splus is the way it
manages its workspaces.  In R when you attach a workspace R will load in
memory the full workspace with all its objects.  This is fine for people
working on small projects and / or small data sets.  When you get into
multiple data sets, multi Giga bytes each, it is silly, in my opinion, to
load all that in memory when you might use only one or two in a given
session.  Further more, this approach is very slow at startup and at shut
down and it eats up a whole chunk of the available memory, leaving a much
reduced memory space for the users.  Splus loads objects in memory upon
request, i.e. only when needed, hence, the workspaces could be huge but
you'll pay the price, time and memory wise, only for the requested objects.

For me, the only advantage (and this is a big one) R has over Splus is the
availibily of all those packages, giving access to the latest statistical
research has to offer.  If only those packages would seamlessly work in
Splus, TIBCO ...!

Cheers,

There are some attempts at GUI's for R, whether they are nice or not is somewhat in the eye of the beholder.

The ones that come to mind (could be others that I am not familiar with):

Rcmdr, I like this one for intro classes, you can do standard graphs and analyses by clicking on menus and filling in dialog boxes. I can argue both sides.  I kept my Splus directories fairly clean by
simple discipline, and the ability to use the natural file system is a
plus.  Many people's directories, like my teenage son's room and several
colleague's email boxes, are a tornado of clutter.  One can't always
blame the package.

  It is true that forcing everyone to manage object memory by hand leads
to uncluttered workspaces.  But management by hand is, frankly,
primitive.  It's like keeping a bedroom picked up by forcing the
occupant to repack all their clothes in a suitcase each morning.  The
'blob of data' is a consequence of basing R on Scheme, which like all
children of Lisp treats all variables as global and intertwined; there
are no truly atomic objects for it to save as separate files.   The true
R converts of course have come to view this set of leg irons as a
featured item of clothing.

I'm sure) would return to Splus long before returning to SAS.  I don't
see any way that TIBCO can compete with the energy and productivity of
the R community however,  New packages have driven our group's
conversion, and I expect the Mayo Splus license to be dropped in 2-3
years.

Terry Therneau

What types of edits do you want to do on your graphics?

R-Plus by XLsolutions corp allows some basic graphics editing.  Other GUIs such as Rcmdr and Rexcel (and possibly JGR and others) allow the creation and some basic annotation of graphics using menus/dialogs.  Some specialized interactive graphics are available in packages like TeachingDemos, playwith, and others.  Base functions like identify and locator allow placing of graphics elements by clicking.

You can also create a graphic using the xfig graphics device, then edit using xfig/jfig/winfig, or create a svg file (cairo device, possibly others) and edit using Inkscape or others.  On Windows you can create metafiles, copy them into word or powerpoint, and from there edit fonts, labels, etc.

There is a package working on creating pgf graphics for use with LaTeX so that the graphs have the same font and other styles as the rest of the document, the most common/legitimate editing of graphics.

Note that interactively editing graphics seems easier than writing a script to create the correct graphic to begin with; until the 3rd time that the client comes back with another data entry error that needs to be fixed and have the graphic recreated with the now "correct" data.

All,
Back to the main question, The future of Splus.

I see SpotFire as a new way and as an opportunity for Splus/R users to deploy analytics, and provide solutions under a corporate environment.  For me it creates a big opportunity within any company that uses SpotFire.  We all know a big drawback from using interpreted languages is the speed limitation and/or integration with Excel.  I mention Excel because there is a lot of legacy work done in Excel, and converting those users to scripted language, Splus/Matlab/R, is a heroic task.  Therefore, to be able to deploy tools compiled, as in Matlab is an advantage not present in Splus language (not sure about R).  On the other hand, SpotFire offers Data Analysis on the Fly not present in Excel, it may also justify the investment of converting some Excel users, and at the same time be able to interact with DLL files created from C/C++/Matlab or Splus/R analytics, best of both worlds.

and R.

I also would hate to see Splus disappear.  I also prefer the look and feel
of Splus over R.  But my main reason in favor of Splus is the way it
manages its workspaces.  In R when you attach a workspace R will load in
memory the full workspace with all its objects.  This is fine for people
working on small projects and / or small data sets.  When you get into
multiple data sets, multi Giga bytes each, it is silly, in my opinion, to
load all that in memory when you might use only one or two in a given
session.  Further more, this approach is very slow at startup and at shut
down and it eats up a whole chunk of the available memory, leaving a much
reduced memory space for the users.  Splus loads objects in memory upon
request, i.e. only when needed, hence, the workspaces could be huge but
you'll pay the price, time and memory wise, only for the requested objects.

For me, the only advantage (and this is a big one) R has over Splus is the
availibily of all those packages, giving access to the latest statistical
research has to offer.  If only those packages would seamlessly work in
Splus, TIBCO ...!

Hello Glenn,

I am also a long time user of Splus.  Several years ago after struggling
for too long with RAM problems on a 32-bit Windows platform I switched to a
Unix Solaris 64-bit platform running a TRUE 64-bit version of Splus with
24Gb of RAM.  That solved the RAM problems.  After a few years on that
plaform we learned that Insightful, at the time, had no plans to keep
developping 64-bit Splus on the Solaris platform but they did for the Linux
platform.  We then switched to a RedHat Linux box, 64-bit of course, with
48Gb of RAM.  I am happy ever since!

I tested quite extensively the Big Data library for data manipulation and I
agree with you, it is not the way to go, 64-bit is way faster, obviously
since all the manipulations are done in live memory rather than on disk.  I
do all my data manipulation in S+ and I routinely work with 2 to 3 Gb data
sets.  I do fit GLMs on data sets with over 2 million rows and over a 100
variables; I won't try to convince you that it runs in a snap, but most of
the time it does run under 30 minutes elapsed time, often less; the machie
is already 3 years old, a newer machine would probably be faster.  I
couldn't tell if Matlab is generally faster than S+ or not since I don't
have it.

Generally on MS systems  Windows won't allow more than 2Gb for a single
application, I think this could be raised to 3Gb somehow; hence, even if
you have more RAM Splus, or any other application for that matter, it won't
be used.  Furthermore on 32-bit systems you can't address more than 2^32
address' spaces.  I don't think TIBCO has yet a 64-bit version of S+ for
64-bit versions of Windows!  This sort of limit your options but I love the
64-bit Linux version, no GUI though, I use it through Emacs's ESS.

Hope this helps,

I also would hate to see Splus disappear.  I also prefer the look and feel
of Splus over R.  But my main reason in favor of Splus is the way it
manages its workspaces.  In R when you attach a workspace R will load in
memory the full workspace with all its objects.  This is fine for people
working on small projects and / or small data sets.  When you get into
multiple data sets, multi Giga bytes each, it is silly, in my opinion, to
load all that in memory when you might use only one or two in a given
session.  Further more, this approach is very slow at startup and at shut
down and it eats up a whole chunk of the available memory, leaving a much
reduced memory space for the users.  Splus loads objects in memory upon
request, i.e. only when needed, hence, the workspaces could be huge but
you'll pay the price, time and memory wise, only for the requested objects.

For me, the only advantage (and this is a big one) R has over Splus is the
availibily of all those packages, giving access to the latest statistical
research has to offer.  If only those packages would seamlessly work in
Splus, TIBCO ...!

memory the full workspace with all its objects.  This is fine for people

load all that in memory when you might use only one or two in a given

request, i.e. only when needed, hence, the workspaces could be huge but
you'll pay the price, time and memory wise, only for the requested objects.

messages.body_plain:
Your pdf does not look like it integrates to 1, you may need an additional scaling factor.

When you say that you want values between 1 and 100,000, do you want just the integers? Or all real numbers?

There are several ways to generate random numbers from a given PDF, and S/R is probably one of the better/easier tools to use for this.

A simple straight forward way (when it can be done) is to find the inverse CDF of your function, generate uniform random values (runif) and feed those values to the inverse CDF and the results will  be distributed according to your distribution.  If you cannot find the inverse CDF, you can approximate it (approxfun), or use other methods (rejection sampling, importance sampling, MCMC, ...).

Hello all

 

Thanks for continuing the discussion, and providing further input. To answer a few of the explicit and implicit questions here:

 

1.       Many of our customers have found the big data library to be very useful for processing large data sets. For a full description of its capabilities, check out the Big Data User's Guide (provided with S+ as a PDF, and also accessible on the Spotfire Technology Network here <http://stn.spotfire.com/stn/UserDoc.aspx?UserDoc=pdfud/TIBCO_Spotfire_SPlus_Big_Data_Guide.pdf> .). Because the big data library uses out of memory methods (by caching data objects to disk), for small problems it can be slower than purely in-memory methods. Its real advantage is that it can scale to objects far larger than what can fit in memory, and perform analyses on that data.

 

2.       As another poster mentioned, under Windows software programs are typically limited to using 2 GB of memory. This limit can be increased to 3 GB by modifying a setting in the operating system. Please contact TIBCO tech support for details on how to do this.

 

3.       Regarding Windows vs. Linux, we have typically found that since the Linux OS tends to occupy less memory than Windows, somewhat larger problems can be tackled on Linux than Windows (though many users still prefer Windows for the ease of use, etc.).  For similar reasons (reducing memory overhead), we recommend very large analyses be done through the S+ command line application or the S+ Workbench, rather than through the Windows GUI. 

 

Customers who want to tackle the largest problems have been most successful using a combination of Linux 64 bit, the big data library, and optimizing/restructuring their code. The latter is something our Professional Services Group has helped a number of customers do to great effect, and I would be happy to provide an appropriate contact if anyone would like more info.

I also would hate to see Splus disappear.  I also prefer the look and feel
of Splus over R.  But my main reason in favor of Splus is the way it
manages its workspaces.  In R when you attach a workspace R will load in
memory the full workspace with all its objects.  This is fine for people
working on small projects and / or small data sets.  When you get into
multiple data sets, multi Giga bytes each, it is silly, in my opinion, to
load all that in memory when you might use only one or two in a given
session.  Further more, this approach is very slow at startup and at shut
down and it eats up a whole chunk of the available memory, leaving a much
reduced memory space for the users.  Splus loads objects in memory upon
request, i.e. only when needed, hence, the workspaces could be huge but
you'll pay the price, time and memory wise, only for the requested objects.
 
For me, the only advantage (and this is a big one) R has over Splus is the
availibily of all those packages, giving access to the latest statistical
research has to offer.  If only those packages would seamlessly work in
Splus, TIBCO ...!

Hello all

 

Thanks for continuing the discussion, and providing further input. To answer a few of the explicit and implicit questions here:

 

1.       Many of our customers have found the big data library to be very useful for processing large data sets. For a full description of its capabilities, check out the Big Data User's Guide (provided with S+ as a PDF, and also accessible on the Spotfire Technology Network here <http://stn.spotfire.com/stn/UserDoc.aspx?UserDoc=pdfud/TIBCO_Spotfire_SPlus_Big_Data_Guide.pdf> .). Because the big data library uses out of memory methods (by caching data objects to disk), for small problems it can be slower than purely in-memory methods. Its real advantage is that it can scale to objects far larger than what can fit in memory, and perform analyses on that data.

 

2.       As another poster mentioned, under Windows software programs are typically limited to using 2 GB of memory. This limit can be increased to 3 GB by modifying a setting in the operating system. Please contact TIBCO tech support for details on how to do this.

 

3.       Regarding Windows vs. Linux, we have typically found that since the Linux OS tends to occupy less memory than Windows, somewhat larger problems can be tackled on Linux than Windows (though many users still prefer Windows for the ease of use, etc.).  For similar reasons (reducing memory overhead), we recommend very large analyses be done through the S+ command line application or the S+ Workbench, rather than through the Windows GUI. 

 

Customers who want to tackle the largest problems have been most successful using a combination of Linux 64 bit, the big data library, and optimizing/restructuring their code. The latter is something our Professional Services Group has helped a number of customers do to great effect, and I would be happy to provide an appropriate contact if anyone would like more info.

OK, folks.  The second shoe has fallen.  At UIowa the number of folks
wanting to renew their licenses for S-Plus has dropped to the point that
it is no longer economical for the University to get a site license.
That means that the cost for my license would increase from about $50 a
year up to about $800 for an individual research llicense.  

Needless to say, this substantially increases my motivation to move to R
before my current S-Plus license runs out.  So the issue arises what I
have to do to move my various files and objects from S-Plus to R.  I
know what to do for most of them.

a)	Dump the objects in each of my S-Plus "projects" and then reload
them into a new R space.
b)	Each of the models starts with a model call, so if I have saved
the underlying data, at the worst I have to copy out the call to a new
file and "source" the file to recreate the object in R.
c)	Print out my functions and rerun them in R, editing the code for
R/S differences where necessary.
All of this should be easy enough, though a bit of a nuisance.

But the real problem comes with all of the SGR files that I have.  These
fall into two classes
a)	those with no embedded data
